```{=html}
<h2 id='star.phases'>Model seasonal changes in stellar visibility</h2><span id='topic+star.phases'></span>

<h3>Description</h3>

<p>Estimate seasonal opportunities for naked-eye stellar visibility.</p>


<h3>Usage</h3>

<pre><code class='language-R'>star.phases(
  star,
  year,
  loc,
  alt.hor = 0,
  alt.rs = 10,
  solar.alt = NULL,
  k = skyscapeR.vars()$k,
  limit = 6,
  refraction,
  atm,
  temp,
  res = 1/24/6,
  method = c("schaefer", "purrington")
)
</code></pre>


<h3>Arguments</h3>

<table role = "presentation">
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_method">method</code></td>
<td>
<p>Visibility model for first morning and last evening. Defaults to Schaefer. Select &quot;purrington&quot; for the passage-transition rule.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_star">star</code></td>
<td>
<p>Either the star name or a <em>skyscapeR.star</em> object.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_year">year</code></td>
<td>
<p>The year of interest. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_loc">loc</code></td>
<td>
<p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_alt.hor">alt.hor</code></td>
<td>
<p>The altitude of the horizon to consider.
Defaults to zero degrees.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_alt.rs">alt.rs</code></td>
<td>
<p>The maximum altitude of a star's first or last
visibility for it to still be considered to be as rising or setting.
Defaults to ten degrees.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_solar.alt">solar.alt</code></td>
<td>
<p>Solar altitude threshold in degrees. NULL uses
-6 for a horizon, or alt.hor - 6 for coordinate input.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_k">k</code></td>
<td>
<p>Visual extinction in magnitudes per airmass (Schaefer 1986, p. S33). The package adopts 0.2 as a clear-sky baseline. Extinction varies with site and atmospheric conditions (Schaefer 1986, 1993). Defaults to the session value from skyscapeR.vars().</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_limit">limit</code></td>
<td>
<p>The maximum magnitude of a star that can be
visible with the naked eye. Defaults to 6.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_refraction">refraction</code></td>
<td>
<p>Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_atm">atm</code></td>
<td>
<p>Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_temp">temp</code></td>
<td>
<p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p>
</td></tr>
<tr><td><code id="star.phases_+3A_res">res</code></td>
<td>
<p>Spacing of solar altitude samples in days, greater than zero and at
most one. Default 1/144 day (ten minutes). Terrain crossings are refined separately.</p>
</td></tr>
</table>


<h3>Details</h3>

<p>The default uses Schaefer's directional twilight brightness and Hecht's naked-eye point-source threshold for heliacal rising (first morning visibility) and acronycal setting (last evening visibility). On each local mean-solar date the calculation searches the terrain-clear rising branch before noon and descending branch after noon, with the Sun below the astronomical horizon. A transition marks the first qualifying morning following an unsuccessful morning, or the last qualifying evening preceding an unsuccessful evening. Solar altitude, stellar zenith distance and the difference in azimuth determine the twilight background. The limiting magnitude sets the dark zenith reference. Rozenberg airmass and the extinction coefficient attenuate the star. Stellar clearance and extinction use the selected apparent or geometric altitude. Solar altitude in the twilight equation is geometric.
</p>
<p>The passage bands, phase type, heliacal setting and acronycal rising use Purrington's altitude-difference rule on a 365-sample solar-longitude cycle. The solar.alt cutoff and alt.rs passage ceiling apply to this classification. Therefore a Schaefer event marker may lie inside a passage band. Selecting the Purrington method also derives first morning and last evening from the passage transitions. A horizon object must cover all bearings. With coordinates, alt.hor supplies the constant skyline.
</p>
<p>The Schaefer fit was developed for twilight near the horizon. Searches at high latitudes or far from the solar azimuth can extend outside its empirical range. The calculation assumes a clear sky and a fixed observer limit. Moonlight, weather and observer adaptation can affect field sightings. Treat an integrated cluster magnitude as a single unresolved target.</p>


<h3>Value</h3>

<p>A skyscapeR.starphases object. The data and seasons tables describe the passage classification. In metadata, events records the event, schematic day, solar.longitude, local date.julian, method and numeric model.day. Use date.julian with <code>riseset</code> and calendar = &quot;J&quot; to locate a crossing. In Schaefer mode visibility.calendar contains morning and evening flags for each local date in the requested Gregorian astronomical year. local.jd is the Julian day number at 00:00 UT for that date label. The horizon.status field describes clearance from the supplied skyline.</p>


<h3>Accuracy of first and last visibility dates</h3>

<p>Across 56 recorded dates, heliacal rising fell within seven days of 22 of 23 first morning sightings. The median prediction was two days early. Acronycal setting fell within seven days of 21 of 33 last evening sightings. The median prediction was five days late. A week is a practical search window. Larger discrepancies occur, especially at dusk. These results apply to the two tested events. <a href="https://stonexsky.github.io/skyscapeR/manual/heliacal-rising.html#v01-observations">V01 observed dates and scientific checks</a>.</p>


<h3>Workflow checks</h3>

<p><a href="https://stonexsky.github.io/skyscapeR/manual/w02-field-to-sky.html">W02 field-to-sky replay</a> checks the Gacrux event at Skorba West. <a href="https://stonexsky.github.io/skyscapeR/manual/h07-panorama-coverage.html">H07 skyline coverage</a> checks terrain inputs. <a href="https://stonexsky.github.io/skyscapeR/manual/a03-stellar-positions.html">A03 stellar positions</a> checks catalogue propagation.</p>

</p>

</p>

</p>

</p>

</p>

</p>
<p>Krisciunas, K. and Schaefer, B. E. (1991). A model of the brightness
of moonlight. PASP 103, 1033-1039 (equation 14 for extinction airmass).
<a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/132921">doi:10.1086/132921</a>.
</p>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<pre><code class='language-R'>## Not run: 
if (requireNamespace("swephRdata", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ss1 &lt;- star.phases('Aldebaran',-4000, c(35,-8,200))
  
  # One can then look at the star's phase type:
  ss1$metadata$type
  
  # Date range of seasons:
  ss1$metadata$seasons
  
  # Date range of phase-type events:
  ss1$metadata$events
  
  # And plot them:
  plot(ss1)
  
  # You can play with the parameters and see how predictions change:
  ss1 &lt;- star.phases('Aldebaran',-4000, c(35,-8,200), alt.hor=2, alt.rs=5)
  plot(ss1)
}

## End(Not run)
</code></pre>

```
